nameStory: The "blue flag" name comes from this iris's stunning blue-violet flowers that wave like colorful flags in wetland breezes. The scientific name "versicolor" means "variously colored," referring to how the petals display multiple shades of blue, purple, and violet, often with intricate veining patterns that seem to shift in different light.
description: Northern blue flag is a showy wetland perennial that stands 2-3 feet tall with sword-like leaves and gorgeous iris flowers. Each bloom features three large, drooping petals (called "falls") and three upright petals (called "standards") in shades of blue to violet-purple. The flowers emerge from tall, sturdy stems in late spring to early summer, making wet meadows and marsh edges look like they're decorated with natural stained glass. After blooming, the plant produces distinctive three-sided seed capsules.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic iris shape with three large drooping petals marked by yellow patches and dark purple veining, plus three smaller upright petals; flowers are typically 3-4 inches across in blue to violet-purple shades

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Sword-shaped leaves that feel stiff and slightly waxy, growing in flat fans directly from the base; leaves are blue-green and have prominent parallel veins you can feel with your finger

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in distinct clumps 2-3 feet tall, often forming colonies in wet areas; stems are sturdy and feel somewhat triangular when you gently squeeze them

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Distinctive three-sided seed capsules that split open when ripe to reveal rows of flat, brown seeds; capsules are about 2 inches long and feel papery when mature

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Almost always found with "wet feet" - in marshes, wet meadows, or along water edges where the soil stays consistently moist to soggy

habitat: Northern blue flag thrives in New England's wetlands, particularly sedge meadows, freshwater marshes, pond edges, and slow-moving streambanks. Look for it in areas where the soil stays consistently moist or even soggy year-round, often growing alongside cattails, sedges, and red-winged blackbird territories. It's common from sea level up to moderate elevations throughout the region.

seasonality.spring: Sword-like leaves emerge early and grow rapidly; flower buds begin forming in late spring as distinctive pointed sheaths at stem tips.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from late May through July, with each flower lasting just a few days but multiple buds opening in sequence; seed capsules begin developing after flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow-brown and seed capsules split open to release seeds; foliage becomes less prominent but remains visible.
seasonality.winter: Leaves die back completely, leaving only underground rhizomes; look for last year's dried seed stalks poking through snow in known locations.

funFact: Northern blue flag was one of just three iris species used in Ronald Fisher's famous 1936 statistical study that helped create modern data science - so this wetland beauty actually helped invent the mathematical tools we use today for everything from medical research to artificial intelligence!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with yellow iris (a non-native invasive with bright yellow flowers) or southern blue flag (which has narrower leaves and smaller flowers). Remember: northern blue flag has wider, stiffer leaves and larger flowers with prominent yellow patches on the drooping petals - if it's big, blue, and bold, it's likely northern!
contextualKnowledge: Despite the common name "poison flag," northern blue flag isn't deadly but can cause skin irritation and stomach upset if handled extensively or eaten. Native Americans traditionally used it medicinally, but it requires expert preparation. All parts of the plant contain compounds that can be irritating to skin and toxic if consumed.
compareHints: Northern blue flag is much larger and more robust than slender blue flag, which has narrow, grass-like leaves and smaller flowers. Unlike the invasive yellow iris, northern blue flag has blue-purple flowers and is native to our wetlands. Southern blue flag has similar flowers but narrower leaves and typically grows in more southern coastal areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Yellow iris is the only consistently yellow-flowered iris you'll find growing wild in New England wetlands - all our native iris species like northern blue flag have blue or purple flowers.
Japanese Iris differs from Northern Blue Flag by its gray-green (rather than bright green) leaves and reddish-purple flower tones instead of pure blue-purple.
Slender blue flag is much more delicate than the common northern blue flag, with leaves that are dramatically narrower (pencil-width vs.

Unlike its freshwater-loving cousins like northern blue flag (which grows in marshes and pond edges), beach-head iris is the only New England iris that can survive in pure beach sand with constant salt exposure.
Dwarf crested iris is dramatically smaller than all other New England irises - while northern blue flag and yellow iris tower at 2-4 feet tall in wetlands, this woodland species stays under 6 inches.
Unlike New England's native blue flag irises which are tall wetland plants, netted iris is tiny and prefers dry, well-drained soils.
Compared to northern blue flag, southern blue flag typically has broader, more rounded flower petals and slightly wider leaves.
Unlike other New England irises that have blue, purple, or yellow flowers, blackberry lily is the only one with orange, spotted blooms.
Sweet iris differs from New England's native blue flag irises by its sweet fragrance and slightly more purple-tinted flowers.
Siberian iris differs from Northern Blue Flag by having much narrower, more grass-like leaves and more compact growth, while Yellow Iris has broader leaves and bright yellow flowers.
Japanese iris differs from native blue flags by its massive, completely flat flowers and preference for consistently wet, acidic soil.
Unlike our common northern blue flag with its blue-purple flowers or the invasive yellow iris with bright yellow blooms, cemetery iris stands out with pure white flowers.
